title: Huatou Chan
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Chán inquiry is the vajra king's precious sword that cuts through deluded thoughts.

inline.s: Chán inquiry is the vajra king's precious sword that cuts through deluded thoughts.

What is called Chan is the state of being free and self-governing: within, one does not turn with one's thoughts; without, one is not dragged about by objects. Huatou Chan reaches this state through inquiry apart from thought (investigating back to before a single thought has arisen).
To reach the state of being free and self-governing, there are three paths: still the mind and that is bodhi; direct pointing to see the nature; and inquiry apart from thought.

blocks.text: Still the Mind, and That Is Bodhi

inline.s: The sutras and treatises say:
When the mad mind does not stop, stop it, and that is bodhi."
Therefore, simply lay it down at once, and walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are all Chan.
Patriarch Bodhidharma said:
"Not recalling any dharma is called Chan samādhi. If one understands these words, then walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are all Chan samādhi."
Treatise on Awakening the Nature
Mazu instructed the assembly:

"The Way needs no cultivation; only do not defile it. What is defilement? So long as there is the mind of birth and death, and fabrication and striving, all is defilement. If you wish to meet the Way directly, the ordinary mind is the Way. What is the ordinary mind? No fabrication, no right and wrong, no grasping and rejecting, no annihilation and permanence, no ordinary and no holy."
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi)
Lay it down at once, "not recalling any dharma," "only do not defile it" —
these are the most direct and trouble-saving ways of attaining freedom and self-governance, but they suit only those of the very highest spiritual capacity.

blocks.text: Direct Pointing to See the Nature

inline.s: A good spiritual friend

points directly, enabling the student to find the master within (see the nature), and then through ox-herding practice removes the habit-energy of deluded attachment, reaching the state of freedom and self-governance. This was the Chan method before Dahui Zonggao.
For example, the Notes on the Forest of Jewels of the Chan Garden records:

Long ago, Lan'an came to study with Chan Master Baizhang. Bowing, he asked: "This student has come wishing to know the Buddha — which one is he?" Baizhang said: "It is much like riding an ox in search of an ox
(your own nature is the Buddha, so why speak of coming to know the Buddha)
." He asked: "After knowing it, what then
(after seeing the nature, what then)
?" Baizhang said: "It is like a man riding an ox back home
(cultivating from the nature, so that the nature returns to its origin)
." He asked: "From beginning to end, how should one sustain it
(on the way home, how should one sustain it from beginning to end)
?" Baizhang said: "Like an ox-herd who, staff in hand, keeps watch and does not let it trample the crops
(in meeting circumstances, cutting off habit-energy thought by thought)

[The habit-energy of deluded attachment] This is the habit-energy by which sentient beings have, since time without beginning, taken the illusory for the real, and so have been driven through birth and death.

The maiden Āmrapālī asked Mañjuśrī: 'I clearly know that birth is a dharma of non-birth — why then am I carried along by birth and death?' Mañjuśrī replied: 'Because your power is not yet sufficient.'

(Translation: The maiden Āmrapālī asked the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: 'Clearly knowing that birth is the dharma of non-birth, why am I still carried along by birth and death?' The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī answered: 'This is because the power to extinguish deluded attachment is not yet sufficient.' For details, see the article
On Birth and Death

By the Southern Song, people's spiritual capacity had grown base and inferior. Unable to prevail over deluded thoughts in ox-herding practice, it became ever more difficult to reach freedom and self-governance through seeing the nature and then removing habit-energy by ox-herding. Therefore Dahui Zonggao (
) vigorously advocated investigating the huatou,
using inquiry to block the mind-consciousness so that deluded thoughts cease to operate — cutting off deluded thoughts
. Huatou Chan quickly became the mainstream of the Chan school, and so it has remained to this day.

The reason huatou Chan is so welcomed by Chan practitioners is this: the method is keen, direct, and single in its focus. So long as one leans upon a single huatou (without needing to attend to anything else), arouses the doubt-sensation, and investigates it to the end, one can break through the afflictions and end birth and death. This is truly a wondrous method of genuine practice and genuine awakening — as the saying goes, "the great Dharma is supremely simple."
Patriarch Huangbo instructed the assembly:
"If you are a real man
(a person of capability)
, look into a gong'an. A monk asked Zhaozhou: 'Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not?' Zhaozhou said: 'Wu (No).' Throughout the twelve periods of the day,
look at the word 'Wu'

. Investigate it by day, investigate it by night; in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; in putting on clothes and taking meals, in shitting and pissing — attend to it with every thought, and summon your energy with full vigor
(rouse your spirits)

: guard the word 'Wu.' As days lengthen and months deepen, it will fuse into one seamless piece, and suddenly the mind-flower bursts into bloom, and you awaken to the pivotal point of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Then you will no longer be deceived by the tongues of the old masters of the world, and you will open a great mouth: Bodhidharma's coming from the West — raising waves where there is no wind; the World-Honored One's holding up the flower — a complete defeat. At this point, what of King Yama, and even a thousand sages will be unable to do anything to you! Do you not believe that there truly is
(there really is)
this
(this)

kind of wonder? Why is it so? Matters fear the man with a will! The verse says: To be wholly free of the dust of toil is no ordinary affair; hold fast the rope's end and wage this single battle; without a bout of cold that pierces to the bone, how could the plum blossom's fragrance fill the nose?"
(The Essentials of Transmitting the Mind) This instruction opened the first stream of huatou Chan.

[Jingcai (spirit)] Here it means "spirit" or "vigor." [Chenlao (dust of toil)] The mind toiling over objects — another name for the afflictions. [To be wholly free of the dust of toil is no ordinary affair] To be completely free of the afflictions (to cut off entirely the delusions of views and thoughts) is no ordinary matter. [Hold fast the rope's end and wage this single battle] This uses ox-herding as a metaphor: firmly grasp the ox's nose-rope to herd the mind-ox, and the nose-rope is "looking at (probing) the word 'Wu.'" The moment the probing slips away, the mind-ox bolts and runs wild, even eating the crops. Hence one must "hold fast the rope's end and wage this single battle" until the ox is tamed and the man at ease, and even both man and ox are forgotten.
[Xianhe (first stream)] The Book of Rites

"Record of Learning" says: "When the three kings sacrificed to the rivers, they all sacrificed first to the Yellow River and only then to the sea." The ancients held that the Yellow River was the source of the sea, so when emperors sacrificed, they first sacrificed to the Yellow River and then to the sea. Later, "first stream" came to denote the thing that first initiates or pioneers.

Later, what Dahui Zonggao most vigorously advocated was precisely this "looking at the word 'Wu'" — taking the word "Wu" as the huatou. There are also many, many other huatou, such as "the cypress tree in the courtyard," "three pounds of hemp," "a dried shit-stick," "the dog has no Buddha-nature," "put it down," "Mount Sumeru," and so on.

The Chan practitioner takes up any one of these huatou, lodges it in the chest, and silently investigates it, thereby blocking the mind-consciousness so that deluded thoughts cease to operate. In time the huatou gains strength, and suddenly, with a resounding "crack!" — like a bean bursting in cold ashes — the nest of ignorance and karmic consciousness is pressed and shattered to pieces, and one sees the mind and realizes the nature.
[Kejiu (
kē jiù
)] An old rut, a set pattern. [Za (
zā
)] To press, to squeeze.

blocks.text: Who Is It That Recites the Buddha's Name?

inline.s: However, for a Chan practitioner even to see the mind and realize the nature is already difficult enough. After seeing the mind and realizing the nature, one must still do the work of preservation and sustainment until the delusions of views and thoughts are entirely cut off, and only then can one end birth and death — this is truly difficult upon difficult. Hence to end birth and death by relying solely on investigating the huatou is as rare as phoenix feathers and unicorn horns.

[The delusions of views and thoughts] The delusions of views and the delusions of thoughts. The delusions of views are the erroneous views of ordinary beings — the five wrong views of the view of a self, the extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of grasping at precepts and prohibitions. The delusions of thoughts are the erroneous thoughts of ordinary beings — the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, arrogance, and doubt. These two kinds of delusion are the root cause by which sentient beings drift through the three realms and undergo birth and death in vain; cutting them off enables one to end birth and death and leave the three realms. [The three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of lust and food — from the six desire-heavens above, through the four great continents inhabited by humans and animals in the middle, down to the Avīci hell below, all belong to it. The form realm is the world inhabited by beings without the two desires of lust and food but still possessing form — the eighteen heavens of the four dhyānas all belong to it. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings with neither form nor appearance, whose minds rest in profound meditation — the four heavens of emptiness belong to it. These three realms are all the states in which ordinary beings pass through birth and death, and therefore Buddhist practitioners take leaving the three realms as their aim.

Therefore, in the Ming dynasty the patriarchs Chushan Shaoqi, Dufeng Benshan, Tianqi Benrui, and Hanshan Deqing began to advocate investigating "who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" — because this takes the Buddha's name as the huatou. If a Chan practitioner possesses the faith and vows to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, then so long as he accomplishes the return of the ten thousand thoughts to the One (this is the Pure Land school's one mind undisturbed), at life's end he is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and thereby end birth and death.

For Chan practice, however, the return of the ten thousand thoughts to the One is only the initial stage of the work and is easy to accomplish; compared with cutting off the delusions of views and thoughts, the difference in difficulty is like that between heaven and the abyss. Hence investigating "who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" became the mainstream of the Chan school from the Ming dynasty onward
, known as the gong'an of verifying the Buddha-recitation, while the Pure Land school calls it Chán-inquiry Buddha-recitation.

In the several hundred years since investigating "who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" became widespread, many have investigated it, few have persevered, and fewer still have finally attained accomplishment. Thus a view has formed: that investigating "who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" is something only those of good spiritual capacity can do.
In fact, this view is mistaken.
The reason that "

many have investigated it, few have persevered, and fewer still have finally attained accomplishment" comes down to two causes. First, without first laying the foundation, they forcibly investigated it, so that only those of good capacity could get a grip and persevere. Second,
their understanding of the path was unclear, and they relied entirely on groping their own way forward.
As a result, only those of good capacity could find the road and thereby attain accomplishment, while those practicing blindly and recklessly abounded, with no end result.
The fact is:
so long as one
lays the foundation well, investigates correctly, practices with diligence, and possesses both faith and vows,
then "who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" —
everyone can investigate it, everyone can use it to end birth and death, and of ten thousand practitioners, ten thousand will go.
